transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-11 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Anna Morales (Bluehaven Director of Platform), Devon Park (Bluehaven SRE), Marcus Li (Bluehaven Security), Samir Patel (Bluehaven Staff Eng)

Summary:
Quick demo of Redwood's Live Forensics Inspector (console toolbar + request trace playback) focusing on multi-step error analysis, request logs, and KV cache fallbacks. Customer wants deep dive into how to triage outlier latency spikes and tokenization/embedding mismatches.

Topics: live trace playback, request metadata (headers/route/model), KV cache / prefix caching, fallback routing to quantized models, audit logs and KMS integration, POC scoping for isolated dedicated pool

00:00 Liam (Redwood): Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I think we've got most of the folks—welcome. My name's Liam, AE on the account, with Priya, our solutions engineer.
00:09 Anna (Bluehaven): Hey! Good to see you both. We're excited to see the "Inspector" flow, we had a few incidents last week where customer's responses timed out and then returned partial outputs.
00:18 Priya (Redwood): Great, we'll walk through the console request playback and then jump into a live forensic on one of the failing traces you sent earlier. Quick note: transcription may blip—I'll also share the deck and the trace export after the call.
00:30 Devon (Bluehaven): Quick qual: we're running a mixed fleet; primary inference is on-prem with a hybrid cloud fallback. We need to understand how Redwood's routing and fallbacks behave when, say, a VPC link drops or a dedicated pool is saturated.
00:45 Liam (Redwood): Perfect. That's a common scenario. High-level, Inspector surfaces the routing decisions in the trace timeline—what routed where, cache hits/misses, and any model fallback. We'll show how the console annotates those events.
00:58 Marcus (Bluehaven): Also security question up front: we require KMS envelope encryption and SSO (SAML). Can you confirm we can block any plaintext logs outside our VPC?
01:06 Priya (Redwood): Yes, we support customer-managed KMS and Private planes—uh- private control plane for Private customers. For hosted, we have options to redact payloads and disable trace payload retention; we'll show the audit trail without payloads too.
01:20 Anna: Perfect.

02:05 Priya: Okay, I'm sharing my screen — Console > Inspector toolbar. You'll notice the timeline along the top, with markers for request start, KV cache lookup, model invocation, and response streaming. Each marker expands into a pane with raw request headers, token counts, and latency breakdown.
02:30 Liam: Important to call out: tokenization mismatch can look like a normal "fast" model call but with huge generation loops—so you get token churn. Inspector shows token delta per step.
02:45 Devon: Can you show a real failing trace? The one we uploaded was request ID bh-20260129-xx — it had a 12s tail latency and then a partial response.
02:55 Priya: Pulling that now... okay found bh-20260129-xx. Timestamped events: 2026-01-29T18:11:02Z request start, 18:11:04 KV lookup (miss), 18:11:04.5 route attempt to dedicated-pool-1, 18:11:06 queued in GPU scheduler, 18:11:18 model invocation returned partial chunk and then a socket reset.
03:15 Priya: See here there's a spike in block allocate and a long wait in the scheduler. You can click-through to the per-server logs (we stitch the per-host tail logs when you upload them) — here's the NGINX upstream timeout too.
03:35 Samir (Bluehaven): Hmm, we saw that nginx upstream timeout earlier. But the weird part is sometimes the same request goes to hosted mode and completes fine, is there a routing policy we missed?
03:46 Liam: Yes, smart routing can prefer cost-tiered models; if dedicated pool is at capacity it will fallback to a compatible quantized variant in hosted—unless you pin the model or set strict routing.
03:58 Devon: Can we make the fallback only to our private dedicated pool?
04:03 Priya: You can. In the policy you can set 'strictAffinity': true which prevents fallback, but then you risk 503s if capacity is exhausted. We usually recommend a canary with 'softAffinity' first.

05:10 Priya: Now I'll switch to the request detail pane — it shows request headers, route, model, prompt hash, embedding cache key, and a small waveform of token timing. There's also a "cache diagnostic" that breaks down prefix hits vs KV items. For this trace you see a full KV miss because the prompt included dynamic user context that wasn't prefetched.
05:40 Anna: Is there an automated suggestion for prefetch keys? We have recurring prompt patterns.
05:46 Priya: Yes, Redwood Optimize will suggest prefix/prefetch rules based on your token distributions. We'll generate a recommended prefetch rule set and you can accept or tune. For POC we can surface the top-10 suggested prefixes.
05:58 Liam: Also to note — the console will simulate how prefetching those keys would have impacted the latency. The inspector has a "what-if" toggle that replays the trace with simulated cache hits.
06:15 Devon: Can we run that now?
06:17 Priya: On it — toggling "simulate prefetch"... replaying. You can see the scheduler wait drops from ~12s to ~1.2s in the sim. That's because the model invocation moves earlier in the pipeline.
06:35 Marcus: The sim looks great but we need to be confident in production—any chance of false positives in the suggestion engine?
06:43 Priya: There's a confidence score tied to suggestion frequency and token overlap. We won't recommend something that affects <0.1% of your traffic. We also provide an A/B rollout control so you can validate on a subset.

07:50 Liam: Switching now to the playback step — I'll pause/resume token streaming to show where the partial output was truncated. See at 18:11:20 there's a partial chunk and then socket reset. The inspector correlates that with the underlying host OOM metrics — you can see a CPU and GPU mem bump right before.
08:12 Samir: That OOM is interesting — we thought we sized the instance correctly. Do you capture per-request GPU memory allocation?
08:20 Priya: We capture per-inference approximate allocation and peak usage. It's an estimate but typically within 5–10% of observed values on the host. For dedicated pools we surface more granular metrics if you opt-in to per-request telemetry.
08:40 Devon: We are cautious about per-request telemetry for PII reasons; is the telemetry encrypted?
08:47 Priya: Telemetry streams are encrypted in transit and at rest; for Private customers you can route telemetry through your collector. We also have a redact policy for payload contents in traces.

09:30 Liam: Quick pause — any more security questions?
09:33 Marcus: Yes—audit logs. Can you show where who-called-what is stored?
09:38 Priya: In the audit pane — here — you have immutable events: model deploy, config change, routing policy update, and per-token quota events. Exports are available to your SIEM via S3 or syslog.
09:50 Marcus: Good. Also, support for customer-managed KMS? You mentioned.
09:54 Liam: Yes, we support bring-your-own-KMS for encryption of persisted traces and model artifacts. We'll include the KMS integration doc in the follow-up packet.

11:05 Priya: Back to the trace — I'm going to open the raw request log. You can filter by header, by user id, or by tokenization boundary. Note the tokenizer here split the user context differently because they had an emoji included—emoji often causes token expansion on some tokenizers, which explains the token churn.
11:30 Samir: Wow. We actually saw some Unicode shenanigans. How do we normalize tokenization across models?
11:38 Liam: You can apply a pre-tokenization normalization on the client side or pin models to a tokenizer schema. It's a tradeoff; normalizing can affect model understanding in rare cases.
11:50 Devon: Can Redwood surface a per-model tokenizer diff?
11:52 Priya: Yes, in the model catalog there's a tokenizer preview — shows token boundaries for sample inputs. We'll show that in the follow-up link.

13:10 Priya: Now, I'll demonstrate how we correlate request logs with infra metrics. Click the "stitch logs" toggle — this requests the logs you provided earlier and overlays host-level logs with the timeline. See how the NGINX timeout aligns with the scheduler queue spike? That suggests a downstream bottleneck rather than the model itself.
13:40 Anna: In this case, NGINX was upstream-proxying to your sidecar that does batching. Could the batching logic be reconfigurable? We saw situations where very short requests get pooled and wait.
13:52 Priya: Yes, batching controls include batch window, max tokens per batch, and a priority exemption list. For latency-sensitive routes you can exempt requests under X tokens to bypass batching.
14:10 Devon: Exemption seems useful. Do you have a recommended starting point?
14:14 Priya: For most teams we set a 5ms batch window with an exemption for requests under 64 tokens. But it depends on the distribution — Optimize will recommend values.

15:30 Liam: Moving on to fallbacks — here's an example of a route that fell back to a quantized model in hosted land. The inspector flags the fallback with a yellow ribbon and shows the cost/latency delta.
15:44 Samir: Quantized variants introduce hallucination risks for us. If we fallback, is there a policy to require output verification?
15:52 Priya: Yes, we have a post-processing validation step you can opt into that runs an eval on outputs (e.g., reranker or heuristic checks). You can configure thresholds that trigger a re-run on the higher-fidelity model.
16:12 Devon: That could be expensive. Can we limit re-run only for high-risk flows?
16:18 Priya: Exactly — tag your sensitive flows and only apply verification there.

17:40 Liam: I'm going to trigger a live replay with redaction enabled — this will hide prompt tokens but still show timing and route. This is useful for security reviews where you don't want payloads.
17:55 Marcus: Works for us.

18:30 Priya: Slight tangent — on the SDK side we provide hooks to emit a request-level trace id. If you instrument that id through your services, Inspector will stitch traces across your services and ours and give you end-to-end latency maps.
18:46 Anna: We already have a trace id in X-Request-Id but haven't passed it into the inference call. Is that a small change?
18:52 Liam: Small SDK change, yes—most customers add it in a single line. We'll include a patch in the follow-up.

20:00 Priya: Let's talk about forensic export: you can export a trace with three privacy modes — full, redacted, and metadata-only. For compliance audits we recommend metadata-only plus an encrypted export to your S3.
20:18 Marcus: For audit we need retention logs for 2 years. Is that supported?
20:22 Liam: Yes, long-term retention is an enterprise add-on; data residency options apply. We'll include pricing in the follow-up packet.

21:30 Priya: Ok, demoing another feature — "request clusters". Inspector can group similar failing requests to show whether an issue is systemic or a one-off. Here's a cluster view — this cluster has alternating tokenization spikes, pointing to an upstream normalization error.
21:50 Samir: That clustering looks extremely useful to prioritize fixes. How are clusters defined?
21:56 Priya: We use a mix of edit-distance on prompt text, tokenization deltas, and route similarity. You can tune thresholds.

23:10 Liam: Timebox check — we've got about 30 minutes left. Any must-see features?
23:15 Anna: Could you show the scheduled alerting and regression detection? We want to be notified before a big SLA hit.
23:21 Priya: Sure — Optimize's regression detector runs evaluation sets you provide and will open a regression alert if key metrics (latency, avg token churn, hallucination rate) deviate. Alerts can post to PagerDuty/Slack and include the top failing traces.
23:40 Devon: Can we auto-open a ticket in our JIRA with the failing traces?
23:44 Liam: Yes, we can POST to your ticketing system; we include a prefilled issue template with links to the traces.

25:10 Priya: Demoing the runbook generator now — from a trace, the console suggests triage steps: check KV prefetch, check upstream timeouts, verify model pinning. Each suggestion maps to runbook snippets and likely owners. You can customize the runbook per team.
25:40 Anna: That will speed our oncall. Nice.

27:00 Samir: Two quick technical Qs: 1) Do you support per-request isolation for PII-sensitive flows? 2) How does the GPU scheduler prioritize interleaved short vs long requests?
27:14 Priya: 1) Yes — we can provide per-request isolation using dedicated pods and encryption-in-flight; that's part of the Private offering. 2) Scheduler uses age-based prioritization with preemptible slots for short-latency requests; you can tune depending on SLAs.
27:36 Samir: Any documentation on scheduler heuristics?
27:39 Priya: I'll drop the scheduler whitepaper after the call.

29:00 Liam: All right, let's hammer out the POC scope. You're asking for an isolated week-long POC to validate inspector triage and routing behavior on your mixed fleet, correct?
29:12 Anna: Correct. We'd like dedicated pool capacity to mirror our on-prem heavy tail, and then run a playback of last month's 10k requests.
29:21 Liam: Two clarifications — 1) do you want model parity or a compatible quantized variant for cost reasons? 2) Do you want telemetry forwarded to your collector or Redwood's console only?
29:31 Anna: For parity, initially parity would be ideal for confidence; if costs are prohibitive we can consider quantized variants later. Telemetry: we'll want copies forwarded to our collector (Splunk) and minimal payload retention in Redwood.
29:44 Liam: Sounds reasonable. We'll propose a POC config with dedicated pool (X GPU cards), parity model, and telemetry forwarding.

31:05 Priya: Quick demo of the error analysis export — generating a POC packet now: included are the config template, runbook snippets, and a sample of simulated prefetch rules.
31:20 Devon: Awesome, can you also include expected cost estimates for the POC?
31:24 Liam: Yes, we'll include a detailed cost table and an assumptions sheet.

33:00 Priya: Showing one last feature — "time travel" replay. You can replay a trace and step through the scheduler and model internals with a slider. This is helpful to see race conditions.
33:16 Samir: Very helpful. That should make RCA much faster.

35:00 Anna: Anything else we should be aware of with Private deployment timelines? We have procurement gating and want to align with their rhythm.
35:10 Liam: Private on-prem deployments typically take 6–8 weeks after contractual sign; VPC options are faster (~2–3 weeks) depending on your networking approvals. We can run a hosted POC first while procurement completes.
35:26 Marcus: Procurement will want SOC2 + encryption guarantees.
35:30 Liam: We'll send SOC2 and KMS docs in the follow-up and can set up a security deep-dive with our security team if you want.

37:00 Anna: Great — let's recap next steps.
37:05 Liam: Recap: 1) Redwood to send SOC2 and KMS integration docs (Liam) — due Fri 2026-02-13. 2) Priya to run KV-prefetch simulation on your sample payload and upload test traces — due 2026-02-18. 3) Bluehaven to provide 3 failing request IDs and confirm POC week-of timeframe — due 2026-02-16. 4) Schedule security deep-dive if requested.
37:30 Anna: That aligns. We'll confirm POC week in the next 48 hours.

38:00 Devon: One more nit — do you have an SLA for streaming partial responses? We need guaranteed partial progress reporting for long outputs.
38:10 Priya: Streaming guarantees are part of our SLA for dedicated pools—progressive streaming with chunk ACKs; we'll include the SLA excerpt in the follow-up.

39:45 Liam: Wrapping up — I'll send the POC packet and a calendar invite for a kickoff. Any final questions?
39:53 Marcus: None from me.
40:00 Samir: No. Thanks.

40:10 Liam: Thanks everyone for the time. We'll follow up with the artifacts and sync on POC scheduling.

End of transcript.
